title: Building the Test Framework You Have Been Using

questions.question: A test file contains no call to a register function, yet every test runs. How?
options: Each test creates an object at file scope whose constructor registers it before main
The compiler scans for functions whose names begin with test
The linker collects them automatically
The build system generates a main that calls each one
questions.explanation: File scope objects are constructed before main is entered, and the framework exists to exploit exactly that side effect.

questions.question: Why is the registry a static local inside a function rather than a global variable?
options: Globals cannot hold vectors
So the registry can be reset between runs
It makes the registry faster to access
The order of construction between translation units is undefined
questions.explanation: A registrar could run before a global was built. A static local is constructed the first time control reaches it, which is necessarily before its first use. That is the standard cure for the static initialisation order problem.

questions.question: Why does MINI_TEST end without a closing brace?
options: To allow several tests to share a body
So the block written after it becomes the body of the generated function
Because the preprocessor adds one automatically
Because macros cannot contain braces
questions.explanation: The macro expands to a declaration, a registrar, and the start of a definition. The learner's braces complete the function.

questions.question: What does #expr do inside a macro?
options: Pastes it onto the previous token
Evaluates the expression twice
Turns the expression into a string literal
Marks it as a preprocessor directive
questions.explanation: A failure can print the code. Stringification is why a report can say expected this to be true: 1 == 2, rather than only reporting that something was false.

questions.question: Why must run_all clear the recorded failures before starting?
options: So calling it twice reports the same result rather than accumulating
Because failures are stored in a fixed size buffer
To free memory between runs
So that tests can be run in a different order
questions.explanation: A framework whose answer depends on how many times it has been asked is not much of a framework, and the lesson's tests check exactly this.

questions.question: When should a check be a require instead?
options: Only in tests that touch hardware
When its failure makes the following lines meaningless or dangerous, such as a size before indexing
Whenever the value is important
Whenever the check involves a pointer
questions.explanation: This rule came from a real bug in this repository: a size check failed, execution continued into the read, and the learner saw a crash instead of a sentence naming the problem.
